title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 101: Notice of meeting

content.overview: Section 101 ordinarily requires clear 21 days’ notice of a general meeting, specifies what the notice must state and identifies the persons entitled to receive it. Shorter notice is possible only with the consent specified by the section.
content.glance: Give clear 21 days’ notice, state place/date/day/time and business, and serve each statutory recipient. Shorter notice requires the section’s prescribed consent.
content.study:
## Notice period and shorter notice
A general meeting may ordinarily be called by giving not less than clear 21 days’ notice in writing or through prescribed electronic mode. The section permits shorter notice only if consent is given in writing or electronically: for an AGM, by at least 95% of members entitled to vote; for another general meeting, by the prescribed majority in number and members representing at least 95% of the relevant paid-up voting share capital, or by members holding at least 95% of total exercisable voting power where there is no share capital. Apply the statutory text to the company’s circumstances and resolution-specific voting entitlement.

## Contents and recipients
The notice must specify the place, date, day and hour of the meeting and state the business to be transacted. It must be given to every member, the legal representative of a deceased member or assignee of an insolvent member, the auditor(s), and every director. An accidental omission to give notice, or non-receipt by an entitled person, does not by itself invalidate the proceedings under section 101(4); do not treat that limited rule as curing deliberate or material non-compliance.

## Practical verification
Preserve the notice, dispatch/service evidence, recipient list, consent records and meeting particulars. Check the applicable rules, articles, statutory exemptions and any special provision governing the meeting.

sections.heading: Ordinary notice period
sections.body: The default is not less than clear 21 days’ notice, in writing or through the prescribed electronic mode. Count the period under the applicable rules rather than assuming calendar-day arithmetic without checking the governing method.

sections.heading: Shorter notice consent
sections.body: For an AGM, consent is required from at least 95% of members entitled to vote. For another general meeting, apply the section’s distinct voting threshold for companies with share capital and without share capital.

sections.heading: Contents and statutory recipients
sections.body: The notice must state place, date, day, hour and business. Give notice to members, the relevant legal representative or assignee, auditors and every director as section 101(3) requires.

sections.heading: Accidental omission and proof
sections.body: Accidental omission or non-receipt does not alone invalidate proceedings under section 101(4). Keep reliable dispatch and consent records and separately test whether any alleged omission was genuinely accidental.

provisions.title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 101: Notice of meeting

examples.title: Compliant notice
examples.body: The company gives clear 21 days’ notice with the required meeting particulars and business to all statutory recipients. Subject to rules and other applicable requirements, the section’s ordinary notice requirement is addressed.

examples.title: Shorter notice without consent
examples.body: The company calls a meeting at short notice but cannot establish the percentage of written/electronic consent required by section 101. The meeting cannot be treated as compliant merely because some members attended.

hypotheticals.question: A company calls a general meeting on less than clear 21 days’ notice. It asserts that enough members agreed, but its records do not distinguish AGM consent from consent for another general meeting. What should counsel examine?
hypotheticals.analysis: Identify the meeting type, voting entitlements and capital structure; apply the correct consent limb in section 101(1); inspect written/electronic consents and the notice particulars; verify recipients and service records. Attendance alone does not replace the statutory consent test.

distinctions.title: Section 101 and connected meeting-compliance requirements
distinctions.right: Section 101 regulates notice and consent. Section 102 addresses information that must accompany notice for special business; section 103 separately determines whether quorum exists.
